What difference does it make to add a bunch of zeroes to a coin value?

Usually currencies start in ranges easy for people to calculate in. But then the money looses it's value and they introduce higher notes. That's usually caused by the state having high debts in it's currency and the central bank creating more money to pay for that. Increasing the supply causes the value to drop. Such a thing would be an option for Greece if it weren't using the euro and that's why the "grexit" is sometimes talked about.

Each country has its own currency so that it has the option of manipulating the value of their currency to fit the economic or political needs at any given time. For example, a lower value currency can be beneficial for a country that has a lot of exports, while a currency that is gaining value will see increased domestic spending.

With the common Euro as the currency of the Eurozone countries, any changes deliberately made to the value of the Euro have to be agreed upon by all the members of the union. As a result, the Euro's value usually lies somewhere in the middle of the needs of every country in the Eurozone, which is a contributing factor to Greece's current debt situation

I think what you're describing is known as redenomination, which simply shifts the scale (usually down to smaller numbers) of a currency. For example, if Japan were to reassign their Yen so that 1 "New Yen" equals 100 "Old Yen" to make the Yen a closer representation of the USD or for whatever reason.

This has no real effect on the value of the currency, but is usually a way of, as /u/xyzzy mentioned, placing the currency back in a manageable range of numbers. This is usually done in response to super- or hyperinflation to keep the exchange of money convenient (so you're not lugging around sacks or wheelbarrows full of bills to buy a loaf of bread)

Simple DirectMedia Layer is a cross-platform development library designed to provide low level access to audio, keyboard, mouse, joystick, and graphics hardware via OpenGL and Direct3D.

Here's a StackOverflow question about the difference between frameworks and engines.

In this context, you can think of SDL as a framework that has interfaces for the raw system calls for input, graphics, etc. You tell SDL to draw a picture on screen and it figures out how to do it on Windows, Linux, or a Mac without you having to worry about the differences between platforms, which would require a huge amount of rewriting otherwise.

The majority of engines and frameworks don't rely on SDL, they usually do their own implementations for the raw system calls for each platform. However, there are some frameworks that do rely on SDL, pygame being one of them.

I'm currently building a game engine using SDL2. I'm doing this as a learning process, so I admit my ignorance and can be totally wrong about how I'm going about this.

But anyway, from my experience, SDL is just a middle-ware library to abstract things like input devices, windows mangers, sound devices, etc. Things which can be different from system to system. For instance, Windows, Mac, Linux, Android, all use different windows managers, drivers, etc. All with different methods of controlling them.

SDL is just a way to provide a common interface for the programmer so he doesn't have to write a separate code base for windows and a completely different code base for Linux.

So SDL isn't a game engine. It's a middle-ware library. You use this library to make writing your game engine more consistent.
Does that mean you don't need to make an engine in SDL in order to make a game (in SDL)?

I'm not sure I entirely understand your question.

Your game is going to need an "engine" of some kind. The term "engine" is loosely defined. But generally all it means is "The code which makes your game a game". SDL is not an "engine". It is just an I/O middle-ware library.

So, no, you don't specifically need SDL. You can use GTK (for linux) or whatever windows manager Window and Mac are using these days. But, you'd have to write a different code base for each platform, as each OS uses a different API to draw windows.

So, for instance, in the Linux world, we are transitioning from the decades old X Windows Server to a new server called "Wayland". Developers who didn't use SDL are going to have to rewrite their code to be compatible with Wayland. However, SDL acts as a middle-ware for the developer, so someone using SDL won't have to worry about incompatibilities when the switch happens. SDL takes care of the differences automatically.

But if you are going to use SDL, you are going to have to write the "engine" of some kind yourself. Why? Because SDL lacks "The code which makes your game a game". All it does is provide a common I/O framework by which you can write cross-platform code.

SDL really has absolutely nothing to do with games, specifically.
